newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New strikes as parents end Belgian sex case appeal.
newsitem.headline: New strikes as parents end Belgian sex case appeal.

text.p: A fresh wave of protest strikes erupted around Belgium on Wednesday in support of parents of child sex and murder victims whose plight has united the linguistically divided nation in horror.

But as hundreds of people stopped work from Arlon in the south to Antwerp in the north, the parents of two of the four girls who have been found dead since mid-August dropped their appeal against a decision to take a key magistrate off the case.
"The appeal has been dropped, but I will make no further comment," Michel Collet, the brother of Carine Russo whose eight-year-old daughter Melissa was among the dead, told Reuters.

Belgium's top court ruled on Monday that magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte had to drop the so-called Dutroux case because he had shown bias by attending a spaghetti dinner organised by a group helping the parents of missing children.
Connerotte, whose job as an investigating magistrate is to build a balanced case file both for and against prosecution, has become something of a national hero for his running of the case.

The decision prompted a wave of spontaneous strikes, stoppages and demonstrations in both halves of linguistically divided Belgium in a show of national unity unseen since popular King Baudoin died suddenly in August 1993.

Public confidence in the Belgian legal system, already at a low ebb from a stream of revelations connected to the case, was further battered by the removal of Connerotte which fuelled theories of a high level cover-up.

The parents of Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo, the eight-year-olds who died while in the hands of a paedophile gang led by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, promptly lodged an appeal against the decision.
But after meeting Justice Minister Stefaan de Clerck they suddenly withdrew the motion.

De Clerck, who said he had learned of the decision from media reports, told a parliamentary committee on Wednesday he had told the parents that after extensive consultations he had concluded reinstating Connerotte to the case was impossible.

He insisted that no pressure had been put on the families to drop their appeal, and said 350 people were now working on the case, conducting inquiries and studying 5,000 pornographic video tapes that have so far been seized.
Even before the decision to remove Connerotte from the case the parents of some of the dead and missing children had planned a march through Brussels on Sunday October 20.
Collet said that judging by the number of calls and letters they had received from all parts of the country there would be well in excess of 50,000 people at the march.
"It is impossible to say just how many people will be there, but I think 50,000 will be a substantial underestimate," he said by telephone from Liege. "This issue has crossed the language barrier."
Belgian railways is offering subsidised return tickets to Brussels from any station in the country for Sunday.
